summary: Weekly POC sync focused on throughput tuning. Observed baseline throughput ~1.9k responses/hr at concurrency 12 with avg p50 latency ~320ms; tail latencies spike under burst. SE recommended increasing concurrency to 24 per GPU (96 total) or intermediate 48 total, tuning batch_timeout_ms to 15-25ms (try 20ms), enable prefix KV caching for repeated prompts, and try priority queueing for low-latency traffic. Agreed to run 4-hour soak and provide logs + dashboard before next sync.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-04-09
Start time: 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Samir Rao (Redwood Eng Ops), Carlos Gomez (BrightCart CTO), Emily Rivera (BrightCart Infra Lead), Liu Zhang (BrightCart ML Eng), Asha Patel (BrightCart PM)
---
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is Jordan from Redwood, I'm the account lead. Quick check — Maya from our SE team is here and Samir is on for the ops side. How's everyone at BrightCart?
[00:07] Carlos: Good, thanks. Busy week but excited to talk throughput.
[00:10] Emily: Hi all, ready to dig into the numbers.
[00:15] Jordan: Cool. Agenda — quick baseline recap, SE tuning suggestions for continuous batching and concurrency, discuss queueing/backpressure, then agree next steps.
[00:23] Maya: I'll jump in with the numbers we got from the last run. So baseline with current config (concurrency target 12, batch_timeout_ms 50, max_batch_tokens 2048) — we saw about 1.9k responses per hour for the mixed workload you shared. P50 latencies around 320ms, p95 ~900ms, p99 spiking up to 2.5s during bursts. GPU util averaged 68%, but we saw a KV cache hit rate only ~12% which is low for your traffic.
[00:48] Liu: That KV number surprised us — we thought reuse was higher. Possible we sanitized the replay too much? The sample has a lot of product name changes.
[00:57] Maya: Yeah if prompts aren't stable the prefix caching won't help. Also tokenization differences can fragment the cache — we saw some prompt variants that blocked reuse.
[01:07] Emily: Can you remind us how Redwood's continuous batching interacts with concurrency? We want to avoid queue buildup that increases tail latency.
[01:15] Maya: Sure. Continuous batching opens a short window (batch_timeout_ms) to collect requests into a single GPU batch. At low concurrency that window can be long if you're waiting for enough requests, adding latency. As you increase concurrent request threads, batches fill faster so you get better GPU utilization and lower per-token cost. The tradeoff is tail latency if bursts exceed concurrency and queue backs up.
[01:36] Samir: Right, so our ops question — what's a safe concurrency target for our Dedicated pool of 4 A100s? We set 12 initially but we can scale.
[01:44] Maya: From the perf model, with your avg sequence length (~120 tokens) and model variant, 24 concurrent inferences per GPU gives more steady batching; for 4 GPUs that maps to concurrency=96 overall. But because you have mix of short chatty prompts and long summary jobs, we usually cap at 0.8x theoretical max to avoid saturation. Practically we recommended starting with 24 per GPU -> 96 total. If you prefer less risk start with 48 total (12 per GPU).
[02:26] Carlos: Hmm 96 feels high; cost and pricing impact are concerns.
[02:30] Jordan: We'll share a pricing delta matrix for those concurrency levels — I can send that after.
[02:34] Emily: Also curious about batch_timeout_ms — you ran at 50ms before, is 50 too high?
[02:39] Maya: For your traffic distribution, 50ms was conservative. Reducing to 15-25ms reduces queuing latency for short prompts. There's a sweet spot: lower timeout reduces p50 but can reduce batch sizes and increase GPU cost; higher timeout increases batch size and lowers unit cost but adds latency. Given your SLA targets (p50 < 300ms for interactive), I'd try 20ms first.
[02:58] Liu: What about max_batch_tokens? We have some summaries that are 800+ tokens — will that starve smaller requests?
[03:05] Maya: Max_batch_tokens should be high enough to accommodate your long tails so they don't block other requests; we suggest keeping it to model max (4096) but enabling dynamic prioritization where small requests go to fast lane. Redwood supports priority queueing — we can put low-latency interactive traffic in a priority queue with a tighter batch_timeout_ms while background summarization goes to a separate queue with longer timeout and larger batches.
[03:30] Emily: That priority queueing sounds ideal. Any caveats for Dedicated?
[03:35] Samir: From infra side, will that require separate worker pools?
[03:38] Maya: Not necessarily separate physical pools; it's logical lanes within the runtime. For Dedicated you can also pin certain workers to a queue for strict isolation. There is a small overhead for managing queues but it's negligible vs GPU work.
[03:50] Jordan: On caching, we think increasing the KV prefix cache hit rate will help a lot with tail reduction. Ideas?
[03:57] Liu: We can normalize product names and canonicalize some prompt templates server-side before replay.
[04:02] Maya: Exactly. Also consider using a short-term keying scheme — e.g., hash of template + user intent — that increases reuse without leaking PII. We'll provide a doc on best-practices for prefix caching.
[04:15] Carlos: For the soak you recommended — what's the exact plan and what do you need from our side?
[04:21] Maya: We propose a 4-hour soak with the following variants: run A: concurrency=48, batch_timeout_ms=20, priority queueing enabled; run B: concurrency=96, batch_timeout_ms=20, caching enabled with your canonicalized prompts. We'll collect p50/p95/p99, GPU utilization, queuing depth, latency distribution, and memory/KV cache hit rate. Please provide the sanitized replay and token hist so we can more accurately mirror production.
[04:48] Emily: We can get the replay uploaded by Friday.
[04:50] Liu: I'll sanitize and remove PII, should be there tomorrow.
[04:53] Jordan: Great. We'll also attach the perf dashboards in the Slack channel.
[04:57] Maya: A note on autoscaling — if you prefer to keep cost in check, set an upper concurrency limit and an aggressive downscale policy with longer cool-down to prevent thrash. Also use warmup pools to reduce cold-starts when batches spike.
[05:10] Carlos: Any change to model quantization suggested? We tested q4 and q5 variants earlier.
[05:15] Maya: Quantization tradeoffs are real — q4 gives very good perf but sometimes slight quality regression on summarization. For mixed workload, we recommend q4 for the interactive lane and q5 for background jobs where quality matters more. That can be enforced via routing policies.
[05:29] Asha: Quick question on observability — can we get token-level cost breakdowns per route?
[05:34] Samir: Yes, Redwood Console gives per-route token and latency breakdowns; we'll share dashboard links.
[05:38] Maya: Also we'll add a tracing hook for sample slow requests so you can inspect model inputs/outputs for regressions.
[05:44] Emily: That will help correlate spikes with certain prompt templates.
[05:48] Jordan: Ok wrapping up — decisions: run soak tests (A and B), BrightCart will provide replay + token hist, Redwood runs soak and shares logs + dashboards, Jordan to send pricing delta. Next sync same time next week unless we need earlier.
[06:02] Carlos: Sounds good. Any other blockers?
[06:05] Liu: No blockers from engineering. Just need the action items and configs.
[06:08] Jordan: We'll capture action items in the doc — Maya will send recommended batching config JSON (note: file may contain parameter names like batch_timeout_ms, max_batch_tokens, concurrency_target).
[06:20] Maya: Quick aside — sometimes transcription messed up our product names in notes, e.g., Redwood Dedicated shows up as 'Redwood Dedicate' in some exports, so please ignore typos.
[06:28] Jordan: Good point. Alright thanks all. We'll follow up in Slack with links.
[06:33] Emily: Thanks everyone.
[06:35] Carlos: Thanks.
